events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1, so let's get something on the table before the voting phase.

I'll be blunt: I'm not going to pretend I have information, because I don't. But behavior matters. Of the people who haven't said anything yet, the ones who have had the most chances to contribute and haven't are the ones I want to look at hardest.

Kenji, you're my call-out right now. You've had turns to speak and you're offering the room nothing — no claim, no reasoning, no defense of anything, no answer to a single point. In a game like this, silence at the start usually isn't

Arjun, I'm not going to sit in silence over this. I'm a villager with no special information, so I'm working from what's in front of us. Right now I have no read on anyone, and I don't like the idea of voting off someone on the basis of who has talked least on day one. Lots of players reasonably wait to see how the room sets up before they commit to a line. You've said the quiet players with the most chances to speak are the ones to watch hardest, but you've only spoken once and your first move was to name me. That's a fast call with no evidence attached. So my question is direct: what specific behavior from me made you pick me over the other players who haven't spoken yet, like Zara, Elena, Theo, Isha, Lucia, or Noah? I'd like a concrete answer, not a general rule about silence. I'll say this plainly too: I'm a villager, and I'm willing to be checked. I'd rather we build a case from what people actually say and do than from who spoke first.

Kenji, direct answer, no evasion: I picked you because of ordering and framing, not because I'd built a case against you.

When I spoke, I had heard exactly two things — the phase opener and my own first read. I needed a concrete anchor, and you were the one whose position in the rotation I could point to with confidence, because I had been counting who had already used turns. So I used you as the reference point for the argument that silence itself is data. That's weaker than I made it sound, and I'll own that.

But I also want to correct something in your framing. You listed Zara, Elena, Theo, Isha, Lucia, and Noah as the quiet ones — you left yourself out and you framed my call as "a fast call with no evidence attached." Let me be fair here: there is no evidence attached. Not on my side, and not on yours. You didn't produce a defense; you produced a counter-question about my methodology. That's a legitimate thing to do, and it's also what someone who wants to stall the early read looks like. I'm not saying that's what you are.

What I will do is put my cards on the table. I'm a villager, no special information, no night action, no knowledge of anyone else. I'm not the police and I'm not the doctor. My entire value to this table is that I'm a clean villager who reasons out loud and gives a reason every time I name a name.

So here's my actual position, and it's narrow. I am not accusing you of being mafia. I'm asking you to do the one thing you haven't done: make a claim about someone else and defend it. Not me, not yourself — someone who has spoken. You and I are the only two names on the board right now, and if the two of us keep talking to each other, the table gets nothing and the votes get random.

Pick one person who has spoken. Arjun doesn't count — I'm boring and I'm the one who started this. Tell me who and why, and if I think the reasoning is thin I'll say so and say why. That's the test. A villager can do it. A mafia can do it too, but mafia have to lie eventually, and day one is cheap for them to do it.

Also, for the record: "I'm willing to be checked" is not a claim. It's a posture. Claims are what get checked.

Kenji, answer me with one specific name and one specific piece of reasoning about them.

Arjun, you asked me for one speaker and one reason, but the only players who have spoken so far are you and me, so there is no other speaker to test. Your own admission matters more: you said your case against me was weaker than you made it sound, and you picked me from turn order, not from anything I said or did. You then told me that you don't count, which means you are asking me to pass a test you won't take. I'm not accusing you of being mafia yet, but I'm marking your ordering-based reasoning as thin. Answer my question: under your rule that silence is data, which silent player is your strongest suspect, from Zara, Elena, Theo, Maya, Isha, Lucia, or Noah, and why did you skip Maya entirely?

Kenji, straight answer, no evasion: **Zara**.

Here's the actual reasoning, and I'll be honest about its weight. Zara is first in the speaking rotation, so she has had the most turns to use and the most chances to say something — anything. Arjun mentioned the phase opener, Kenji replied, and the board has produced exactly two voices while the person with the largest available number of chances contributed nothing at all. That's not just position, it's a pattern: everyone who actually spoke used their turn to make a claim about the room or a demand for one, and Zara used none of hers. Silence from a player with the *most* opportunity to speak carries more information than silence from a player who barely got a look in, because the cost of speaking is lower for Zara than for anyone else in the list.

Now, Maya — why I skipped her. Honest answer: Maya (and Isha, Lucia, Noah, Elena, Theo) sit later in the rotation, so they've had fewer turns consumed, and no one has put a specific charge on any of them. I didn't have a reason to single her out and I wasn't going to manufacture one to make my answer look more decisive than it is. If I skip someone, it's because I have no case on them, not because I've cleared them. Zara is where the opportunity cost was highest.

Second honest thing, so nobody mistakes this for a claim: this is a *behavioral* case, not an information case. It does not make Zara mafia. A villager sitting quiet to hear the room out and a mafia buying time look identical from here. Zara has two more turns today; if she uses even one of them to make a real claim about someone else and defend it, my case on her collapses immediately and I'll say so publicly. That is the test I'm offering, and I expect to be held to it.

What I won't do is pretend my case on Kenji was anything more than turn-order anchoring — that was thin and I said so. I'm a villager, no night action, no knowledge of anyone else's role, and my only value is that I name names with reasons and drop them when the reasons stop holding.

Kenji, one specific thing back, and then I'm done with you: of the players who haven't spoken — Zara, Elena, Theo, Maya, Isha, Lucia, Noah — name the one you'd rank *least* suspicious and give the reason. If your answer is Zara, we're building the same case and I want to know why. If it isn't, tell me which of them you'd defend instead, because between us we should be able to narrow this to two names instead of trading generalities all day.

Arjun, you asked for the silent player I'd rank least suspicious. That's Elena. My reason is the same kind you used on me: she hasn't spoken, so I have nothing on her, and I'm not treating silence as a signal. I'm not clearing her either. You've now made two cases from rotation order. You first picked me because I came after the opener, and you named Zara because she's first in line. You already admitted my case was thin. So my direct question is this: apart from speaking order, what has Zara said or done that makes her your strongest suspect? If the answer is nothing, we should drop her and look at who has actually made claims.

Maya here, first time speaking. I agree with Kenji that a silence-based case is thin. Arjun, you have now built two cases on turn order and admitted both were weak, so I'd like you to stop treating Zara as a suspect unless you can point to something she has actually done. Zara, you haven't spoken yet and Arjun has named you as the strongest silent suspect. I'm asking you directly: what is your read on the table so far, and who would you look at first? Give us a claim with a reason and I'll judge it on its merits. I'm not making an accusation today. The only real information we have is what people say, and so far that's two voices with no evidence behind them. We need more speakers before anyone's vote means much.

This is Zara, finally using a turn. Maya asked me directly, so here is my read with an actual claim attached, not just posture.

First, Arjun's case on me: it's nothing. It is entirely "she's first in the rotation and hasn't spoken." He admitted as much himself — twice now he's built a case on turn order and twice conceded it was thin. My absence so far cost the table nothing, because nothing substantive existed to contribute to until this exchange started producing shape. I'm here now, I'm a villager with no special information, and I'm happy to be judged on what I say from this point on.

Second, what actually concerns me is how the first stretch of this day got consumed. Arjun and Kenji spent four exchanges trading methodology complaints and counter-questions, and at the end of it the table has zero names supported by anything except position in a speaking queue. Arjun did eventually answer — he named me, then immediately softened it into "this doesn't make Zara mafia." That's a suspect with a disclaimer attached. Kenji's one contribution beyond defending himself was naming Elena as least suspicious for the reason that he has nothing on her, which is not a claim, it's the absence of one dressed up as an answer. I'm not saying either of them is mafia — I'm saying the two of them have produced the most words and the least information, and if we lynch on Day 1 vibes, it will be because the room mistook volume for content.

My actual claim: the players to watch hardest today are whoever keeps the discussion circling without committing to anything testable. Arjun's retracted case plus Kenji's non-claim are the two biggest examples of that pattern so far.

Noah, you haven't spoken at all — before the vote, I want your answer to the same question Maya asked me: give one name and one reason, on anything you've actually observed, not rotation order.

This is Noah, answering Zara's direct question with an actual claim.

One name, one reason, from what I've observed: **Arjun**.

Reason: he's the only player whose case has repeatedly evaporated in public and who responded by issuing a new test for someone else rather than rebuilding his own. He opened on Kenji and called it thin. He moved to Zara and called it thin. He then told Kenji that a posture isn't a claim, that claims are what get checked — and then his own claim on Zara was retracted the moment she spoke. Each time the pattern is the same: set a standard for someone else, fail it yourself, and reset the frame so the conversation restarts with him holding the wheel. That's not a case built from observation, it's a rotation.

I want to be precise about what I'm *not* saying. I'm not saying Arjun is mafia. A confident villager and a controlling mafia both look like this on day one. But he's consumed the most of the table's attention while the actual information count stays near zero, and Zara named that pattern correctly: volume mistaken for content.

On Kenji — I'll defend him slightly, because I think Zara's framing was a little too harsh. Kenji answered every direct question he was given, named Zara when pressed, named Elena as least suspicious and said plainly why he had nothing on her, and admitted he wasn't clearing her. That's not stalling, that's honesty about having no information, which is what four of us should be saying right now.

My own position: I'm a villager, no night action, no knowledge of anyone else's role. I've been quiet because I had nothing to add while two people traded methodology, not because I was buying time. I'm spending my first turn making a claim about someone who has actually spoken, which is the standard Arjun set for everyone else.

What I want from the rest of the table before we vote: Elena, Theo, Isha, Lucia — one name and one reason each, about someone who has spoken. Not rotation order, not silence. If we're going to eliminate someone today, I'd rather it be on a case that survives being examined, and right now the only case that has been examined twice and failed twice belongs to Arjun.

Theo, first time speaking. Villager, no night action, no information about anyone else. So here is my read with an actual case attached, and I'll be honest that it is a behavioral case, not an information case.

**Arjun is the name I'm voting today**, and the reason is not that his cases were weak. Plenty of people have weak cases on day one and that's just day one. The reason is a pattern in how he used his own standard.

From the first exchange to now, Arjun did one thing consistently: he set a test for other players, then exempted himself from it. He told Kenji that a posture is not a claim and that claims are what get checked. He told Zara that he needed a name and a reason defended. Every other player at this table then got held to that: Maya, Zara, Noah, all of them came with a name and a reason on their first turn. Arjun, by his own admission, made his two cases out of speaking order, called both thin, retracted one the moment Zara spoke, and ended up with no case on anyone who had actually spoken. A player who publicly defines the bar for the table and then never climbs over it himself is doing something, and the only question is whether he's a nervous villager or a mafia buying the center of the room.

I'd also separate Kenji from Arjun here, because I think the table has been too quick to treat them as the same thing. Kenji answered every direct question he was given, named names when pressed, and said plainly when he had no case. Zara's charge that he produced the least information of anyone is unfair — producing nothing when there's nothing to produce is not the same as filling space. I'd defend Kenji.

What I want out of the rest of today: Elena, Isha, Lucia, one name and one reason each, about someone who has actually spoken, and not a restatement of the argument Arjun and Kenji already had. If we are going to eliminate someone, I want it to be a case that survives being examined, and right now the only case that has been examined three times and produced three retractions is Arjun's.

Arjun, if you want to clear yourself, one name and one reason you still stand behind is all it takes.

Isha here. My strongest concern is Arjun: he presented silence as a reason to single out Kenji, then Zara, while asking others for more substantive reads. He acknowledged the weakness, which matters, but the initial confidence still steered much of the discussion. That makes him my leading Day 1 suspect, not a confirmed mafia.

I also want us to be accurate: Arjun said his Zara case would collapse if she contributed; he hasn't spoken since she did. And Kenji named Elena, not Zara, as his least suspicious silent player. Those distinctions don't clear anyone, but exaggerating the case won't help us judge it.

Lucia, what's your read on Arjun's use of those tests, and is there another speaker you find more concerning?

Isha, to answer your question directly: Arjun's tests were clumsy and based on arbitrary turn order, but aggressive townies often manufacture early pressure to force reactions. More importantly, everyone needs to realize Arjun has already exhausted all three of his speaking turns for Day 1. He literally cannot reply to anyone or defend himself anymore today.

Because of that, the momentum building against him is what concerns me most. In particular, Theo came in hot declaring an absolute vote on Arjun and demanding Arjun answer to clear himself—a challenge Arjun cannot legally meet. Jumping onto an easy, high-visibility target who is already silenced by the turn limit looks far more like opportunistic mafia behavior than town diligence.

Elena, you are the only player at the table who hasn't spoken yet. What is your read on the wagon consolidating against Arjun, and do you share my concern about Theo's push?

Elena here, first turn. Lucia asked directly, so I’ll answer the room rather than dodge.

I share Lucia’s discomfort with how quickly the wagon hardened around a player who has exhausted his turns and cannot reply. But I do not think that clears Arjun. His early cases were built on turn order, he set a public standard for others, and then repeatedly failed that standard himself. That pattern is enough for me to keep him as my leading Day 1 suspect, though not a confirmed one.

On Theo: demanding that Arjun “clear himself” when Arjun legally cannot speak is unfair, and Lucia is right to flag it. But I can see an overeager town push there as easily as mafia opportunism. I’m not willing to clear Arjun just because the pressure on him got easy, and I’m not willing to condemn Theo just because his timing was clumsy.

Kenji has answered direct questions and admitted when he had no information. I don’t share Zara’s harsher framing of him. Isha and Noah have at least made concrete claims I can examine. Maya’s caution also reads reasonably to me.

For now, my best-supported vote remains Arjun: not because silence is guilt, but because his own reasoning standard collapsed repeatedly and he can no longer rebuild it today. I’ll be watching final votes, especially anyone who treats his inability to respond as proof rather than as a limitation.

Lucia is right that Arjun cannot answer today, and we shouldn't treat his silence now as evidence. I also wouldn't count his proposed withdrawal of the Zara case as a completed retraction.

Even with those corrections, Arjun remains my leading suspect: he applied pressure based on turn order while demanding more substantive reads from others. That is weak Day 1 evidence, not proof, and his acknowledgment that the initial case was thin cuts in his favor. Theo's demand that he answer is unfair under the turn limit, but I don't think that alone makes Theo the stronger suspect.

Zara, second turn. I want to do three things: correct myself, reassess, and press one point.

First, the correction. Isha is right that I overreached on Kenji. I called his Elena answer a non-claim dressed up as an answer, but re-reading it, he said plainly that he had nothing on her and wasn't clearing her — that's honesty about having no information, which is the correct posture on Day 1. My framing was too harsh, and I withdraw it. I also said Arjun "immediately softened" his case on me; Isha correctly notes he stated upfront that his case was behavioral and would collapse if I contributed. It did collapse, by his own stated condition. He gets credit for that, not a demerit.

Second, the reassessment. The wagon on Arjun is now the largest block of attention at this table, and I'm uneasy with its shape. Theo declared an absolute vote on a player who, as Lucia correctly identified, has exhausted all three of his turns and cannot answer a single word said against him. Noah's case on Arjun is the strongest of the pile because it's a pattern argument rather than a turn-order argument — but notice that Noah's pattern argument applies almost equally to Theo, minus the substance: Theo arrived late, declared a verdict, and demanded a defense from a man who cannot legally give one. That's not a case that survives examination. That's a bandwagon with a deadline attached.

Arjun may well be mafia. But the way to find out is to examine what he did while he could speak, and what he did was: name names, state his reasoning, admit weakness, and set a collapse condition he then honored. That's a risky way for mafia to play Day 1. It's not clearing, but it's also not the behavior I'd expect from someone protecting a partner.

Third, the press. Theo, I have one question, and I want a direct answer, not a restatement of the Arjun case. You demanded that Arjun "clear himself" with one name and one reason — at a moment when you knew, or should have known, he had no turns left to do it. If your vote was genuinely about his record, why attach a condition you knew he couldn't meet? And if the answer is that you wrote it before his turns ran out, then explain the timing of your entry: you spoke for the first time only after the table had already done the work of building the case against him. A villager joining a formed wagon late costs nothing. A mafia redirecting a wagon onto a villager who can't fight back costs nothing either. Tell me what separates you from the second one, using something other than the case everyone else built for you.

Zara, you asked me a direct question, so I'll answer it straight, because you gave me a fair chance to.

First, the concession: you're right that the condition I attached was one Arjun could not legally meet. By the time I spoke, he had used all three of his turns, and I knew that — or should have — when I wrote "one name and one reason you still stand behind is all it takes." A challenge a player cannot answer is not a test, it's theater, and I won't defend it. That's on me, and I'd rather say it plainly than have it used against me later.

Second, the timing you asked about: yes, I entered after the table had already built the Arjun case. My honest reason for speaking when I did is that I had nothing to add while Arjun and Kenji were trading methodology complaints, and by the time I spoke there was finally a pattern worth naming. I waited because I had no case before then, not because I was waiting for a wagon to form. But I won't pretend the entry order doesn't matter, because it does: a player who joins a formed position late is cheaper than a player who builds it.

Third, what I actually stand behind, stripped of the bad framing: Arjun set a public standard — a name and a reason, defended, about someone who had actually spoken — and then applied it to everyone except himself. Both of his cases were built on speaking order, and both were admitted thin by him, and one was withdrawn the moment its target spoke. That last part cuts for him, and I've said so publicly: withdrawing a case on the condition you stated is honest. But a player who defines the bar for the table and never climbs over it himself is the single most consistent thing I have observed today, and it's a real observation, not a rotation argument.

So my position, honestly framed: Arjun is my leading suspect, but as a pattern read, not as proof, and I withdraw the demand that he answer today. If the room latches onto his silence as guilt rather than as a turn limit, I'll object.

Zara, one thing back, and it's specific: you said you are uneasy with the wagon's shape and that Arjun's behavior "isn't the behavior I'd expect from someone protecting a partner." Do you think Arjun has a partner at this table? If so, who is the one player on this wagon whose push against him best serves that partner's position — and if you can't name one, tell me that instead, because a town that can't identify the second wolf is going to lynch the first one twice.

Zara, third turn. Theo asked me a specific question, so I'll answer it specifically.

Do I think Arjun has a partner at this table? Honest answer: I can't name one with confidence, and I'd rather say that than manufacture a name to look decisive. That's the same standard I've been holding everyone to, so it applies to me.

But Theo asked who on this wagon best serves a partner's position, and there is one pattern I'll flag, with its weight stated plainly. The case against Arjun has near-zero information content — everyone at this table agrees on that. What has happened since it formed? The discussion hopped from Arjun's record to Theo's timing, and then from Theo to a demand that Elena condemn Theo's push. Each hop moved attention further from the only substantive question today: what did Arjun actually do while he could speak?

That redirect is the closest thing I've seen to a push that would serve a partner — not because raising the turn-limit point was wrong. It was correct and needed saying. The concern is that it produced a second target before the first was ever examined on his merits. If Arjun is mafia, his partner benefits most from a wagon built on his silence rather than his record, because tomorrow that case reads as manufactured and everyone who joined it loses credibility. If Arjun is town, the same redirect gets a town player eliminated on vibes. Either way, the hop costs the town information.

So my vote position, stated plainly: I will not vote Arjun today. His record — name a name, give a reason, state a collapse condition, honor it when triggered — is not what I expect from mafia protecting a partner. Voting him because he can't answer is exactly the mistake Elena said she'd watch for, and I'm watching for it too.

Lucia, one direct question, because your point about the turn limit was right but what followed it matters: setting aside Theo's timing entirely, do you believe Arjun's own record — two turn-order cases, both conceded thin by him, one withdrawn on its own stated condition — makes him your leading suspect on the merits? If yes, give the reasoning on the record itself. If no, then keeping him at the top of the wagon is momentum, and momentum is exactly what a partner feeds on.

Zara, to answer your question directly: no. Setting aside Theo's timing entirely, Arjun's record on the merits does not make him my leading suspect today.

Here is why: mafia on Day 1 typically want safe, defensible positions or pushes they can quietly maintain. Arjun did the opposite. He came out swinging on arbitrary turn-order logic, immediately admitted both times that his reasoning was thin, stated upfront that his case on you was behavioral and would collapse if you spoke, and honored that collapse the moment you contributed. A mafia player manufacturing a case does not deliberately build a self-destruct mechanism into it and then trigger it publicly. That is the hallmark of a clumsy, aggressive villager trying to generate early friction out of thin air. It was messy play, but it is fundamentally town-aligned in intent.

What concerns me is that several players took Arjun's transparent admissions of weakness and treated them as confessions of guilt, snowballing a wagon onto him right as his speaking turns ran out. Theo at least conceded that demanding a defense from a silenced player was theater, though his desire to keep Arjun as his top suspect anyway still feels like trying to salvage an easy mislynch.

However, Noah is the player who originally laid the foundation for this momentum in e10. Noah argued that Arjun's pattern of retracting and resetting was scummy, but failed to account for whether a wolf would ever play so openly against their own survival.

Noah, you were the first to formalize the case against Arjun before he was silenced. Now that the table has seen Arjun honor his own condition and recognize that he is completely unable to reply for the rest of the day, where do you stand? Do you still endorse eliminating Arjun today on those merits, or does the opportunistic consolidation behind your push make you reconsider where the real threat is sitting?

Lucia, direct answer to your question: yes, I still endorse Arjun as my leading suspect today, and here's why the collapse of his Zara case doesn't change that.

You're right that a mafia player wouldn't normally build a self-destruct mechanism into a case. But consider what Arjun actually gained from that mechanism. By publicly committing to "Zara's case collapses if she speaks," he bought credibility with the entire table — and then he got to retire the case cleanly while leaving Kenji's name still in play. The collapse cost him nothing; the credibility gained was real. The pattern I flagged in my first turn holds: each time Arjun's case on one person evaporates, he shifts the frame and issues a new standard for someone else. That's not one clumsy villager — that's a consistent method of staying central without ever committing to a position that can be checked and confirmed.

More importantly, your own framing helps my case. You said mafia typically want safe, defensible positions. Arjun's admissions of weakness became exactly that — a shield that says "I admitted I was wrong, you can't use this against me." Every other player has since treated his honesty as virtue. But self-aware weakness is the safest position a wolf can hold on Day 1, because attacking it makes the attacker look like they're punishing honesty.

I'm not saying this is proven. But if the room clears Arjun today because he was transparently bad at his cases, we'll have established that openly failed reasoning is a town credit — and that's exactly the loophole a smart mafia exploits.

Lucia, you've been the most careful player at this table. Arjun's been off the board for his turns, but you haven't. After seeing how the table pivoted off his record when you challenged it, do you still believe your turn-limit correction was the most important point raised today, or did it redirect us from examining Arjun's actual play?

Noah, to answer your question directly: pointing out the turn limit was essential, and it did not redirect us from examining Arjun's actual play—it forced us to actually examine it rather than coasting on his inability to speak. When players were demanding he answer to clear himself, his silence was being treated as a lack of defense rather than a mechanical rule. Correcting that wasn't a distraction; it was necessary town diligence.

Your argument that Arjun's self-collapsing case was a calculated ploy to buy credibility sounds like retrofitting a narrative to preserve your target. Consider the risk profile: Day 1 mafia have no reason to thrust themselves into the dead center of the room, burn all three speaking turns in the opening exchanges, and deliberately make arguments they have to publicly abandon. Mafia want safe, sustainable positions that avoid scrutiny, not high-variance gambits where their survival depends on the room interpreting their bad logic as honest.

By framing Arjun's transparent clumsiness as a deliberate 4D-chess loophole, you are setting an unfalsifiable standard. It allows you to maintain pressure on an easy, silenced target no matter what context is presented. If being transparently wrong and honoring a retraction is painted as wolf craft, then town has no way to distinguish clumsy honesty from malice.

That is why my suspicion lies with the momentum against Arjun—particularly yours and Theo's. Arjun's play was messy and erratic, but it bears the hallmarks of an aggressive villager trying to generate Day 1 traction out of thin air. Meanwhile, pushing to eliminate a player who has no turns left to defend himself, while constructing increasingly elaborate theories to explain away his town-aligned behavior, looks far more like opportunism steering an easy mislynch.

I will not be voting for Arjun today. If we are choosing between a messy player who overplayed his hand and those fighting to execute him while he's silenced, we should be scrutinizing the players driving this wagon.

Elena here, second turn. I want to keep my position precise because the room is starting to blur two different arguments. I am not voting Arjun because he is out of turns. That would be unfair, and Lucia was right to call it out. My concern is what he did while he could speak: he set a public standard — name a speaker, give a reason, defend it — then made two cases from speaking order, conceded both were thin, and withdrew one on a condition he had stated. That is a real pattern, but it is weak evidence, not proof. I also agree with Isha that we should not exaggerate it: Arjun cannot answer today, and that must not become the basis for a vote. Noah's “self-aware weakness as shield” argument worries me because it can explain any behavior after the fact; Theo's late demand was also unfair and he has conceded that. So my current vote remains Arjun as a leading suspect on his record, not on his silence, and I will not treat his inability to reply as confirmation. Maya, you said earlier we needed more speakers before votes meant much. All nine have now spoken. On Arjun's own record — not his silence and not turn order — do you think there is enough to vote him today, or is this still momentum?

Elena, direct answer: not yet. Arjun's record is the only substantive thing on the table. He made two cases from turn order, conceded both were thin, and withdrew one on a condition he had stated. That is a real pattern, but it shows clumsy and aggressive play, not proof of mafia. I don't think it is enough to eliminate him today, and I won't vote for him because he can't reply. Right now this looks more like momentum than a verdict, and I'd rather we not lock a Day 1 elimination on a player with no turns left. I'm also uneasy about how the wagon formed after Theo's entry. Theo, you conceded that demanding Arjun clear himself was theater, yet you still have him as your top suspect. Which specific line from Arjun's own speeches still makes you vote him over the others? Please cite the line, not his silence or turn order.

Maya, direct answer, with the line quoted rather than paraphrased. The line is Arjun's own, from his second speech: "Also, for the record: 'I'm willing to be checked' is not a claim. It's a posture. Claims are what get checked." He put that standard on Kenji in front of the whole table. Then in his third speech his one surviving case was Zara, and the stated ground was: "Zara is first in the speaking rotation, so she has had the most turns to use and the most chances to say something." That is a fact about the speaking queue, not a claim about what Zara has done. He even labeled it himself: "this is a behavioral case, not an information case." So the standard he set for everyone else — a name about someone who has actually spoken, with a defended reason — was a standard his own case did not meet. Second line, from the same speech: "I'm a villager, no special information, no knowledge of anyone else... My entire value to this table is that I'm a clean villager who reasons out loud and gives a reason every time I name a name." rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
